summary: ERRNO is a fault-tolerant medical monitoring hub designed for deep space missions. We developed a rule-based Health Index Engine that evaluates individual crew baselines rather than static thresholds. To address the critical issue of false alarms, our system uses Sensor Fusion to mathematically isolate hardware failures - such as a disconnected wearable - from actual biological emergencies, preventing unnecessary ship-wide panic. We also implemented a Break-Glass security protocol. Crew medical telemetry remains strictly private by default to reduce psychological stress, automatically unlocking for the Chief Medical Officer only when an astronaut's health index drops to a critical state. This architecture provides reliable, autonomous life-support management during communication delays with Mission Control, ensuring crew safety without compromising privacy.

Project Details: ERRNO - Deep Space Medical Hub

1. What it does and how it works ERRNO is an autonomous, fault-tolerant life-support and situational awareness system designed for deep space missions. Unlike traditional medical dashboards that rely on static red/green thresholds, ERRNO operates on a dynamic Rule-Based Scoring Engine. It calculates a unified Health Index (0-100) based on an astronaut’s individual physiological baselines. The system continuously ingests telemetry (heart rate, SpO2, blood pressure, etc.), cross-references it with daily mission hygiene (sleep quality, psychological forms), and applies penalty points only when deviations exceed safe individual limits (Delta).

2. Key Benefits and Sensor Fusion A critical problem in space medicine is hardware failure causing ship-wide panic. ERRNO solves this using a "Sensor Fusion" approach. If a wearable device disconnects or malfunctions (e.g., reporting a pulse of 0 or a body temperature of 25°C), the system mathematically isolates this anomaly. It flags the sensor as "N/A" without collapsing the astronaut's Health Index, thus eliminating false medical alarms.

3. Privacy by Default (Break-Glass Protocol) Constant medical surveillance induces psychological stress on the crew. ERRNO implements a Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and a strict "Break-Glass" security protocol. By default, crew medical data is hidden from peers and the Mission Commander. Detailed metrics are automatically unlocked only when an astronaut's Health Index drops to a critical state (Status 2), ensuring privacy is maintained until a genuine emergency demands intervention.

4. Expected Impact The primary impact of ERRNO is reducing the cognitive load on the crew and Mission Control. By filtering out hardware noise and automating health risk assessments, the system allows the crew to operate autonomously, which is vital during the inevitable 20-minute communication delays with Earth.

5. Tools and Tech Stack The project was built as a full-stack, production-ready prototype:

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, and SQLite (aiosqlite) handle data ingestion, the rule-based scoring engine, and RBAC logic.
  • Frontend: Next.js and React provide real-time role-based dashboards (Astronaut, Commander, Chief Medical Officer) with live WebSockets/TanStack Query updates.
  • Simulation: A custom telemetry generator (running on a separate port) simulates hardware inputs, hardware failures, and Earth-delay scenarios.

6. Creative Factors Considered Our team prioritized architecture over pure UI design. We considered the psychological factors of long-term isolation, which led to our privacy-first approach. We also factored in the harsh reality of hardware degradation in space, which drove the development of our fault-tolerant scoring model, ensuring that a broken sensor does not equal a dead patient.
Note: Super Intelligence (LLM tools) was used to assist with backend logic generation, debugging, and text translation.
